Lessons.Title: Modeling Exponential Behavior
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: choose and critique an exponential model for messy decay measurements, identify approximate factor from several ratios, evaluate residuals and distinguish authentic experiments from fabricated demonstration data. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 11, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/11/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/11/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The publisher's main investigation uses successive ball-bounce heights and data/model critique, not exact perfect decay alone.

Original hypothetical bounce-height observations in centimetres for bounce numbers n=0,1,2,3 are100,61,37,22. These numbers were constructed for mathematical modeling, not measured from a bouncing ball. A simple approximate model is H(n)=100(0.6)^n, predicting100,60,36,21.6cm. Observed-minus-predicted residuals are0,1,1,0.4cm; the model does not fit exactly.

Compare a constant subtraction model L(n)=100−20n, which predicts100,80,60,40 and has residuals0,−19,−23,−18. The exponential model has much smaller absolute errors here. Ratios of actual heights61/100=.61,37/61≈.607,22/37≈.595 vary slightly around.6, making a multiplier around.6 defensible.

Student task: construct graphs with shared scales, compute at least three ratios, propose two potential exponential factors, compare prediction error and explain possible measurement variation. An actual ball experiment is optional, and requires genuine data collection to count as performed. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for transparent data provenance, factor estimation, model comparison and reasoned uncertainty.

KeyConcepts.Title: Approximate factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Messy observations may support a factor near but not exactly constant.

KeyConcepts.Title: Residual
KeyConcepts.Definition: Observed minus predicted quantifies departure from a chosen model.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model selection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare errors using identical observed points before preferring one model.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Avoid claiming a model is exact when residuals remain.
KeyConcepts.Example: Exponential residuals small versus linear subtraction model large.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming every measurement ratio must equal the chosen factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Real data often exhibit noise and rounding.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an approximate fit and residual analysis.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Authored numbers are not actual measurements.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label hypothetical example and leave experiment unperformed unless evidenced.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Judging models based solely on the final point

SummaryPoints: A reasonable approximate exponential model need not pass exactly through each point.
Bounce data here are fictional and model factor≈0.6.
Errors quantify fit and help compare alternatives.
Teacher reviews actual experiment claims and argument.
